title: Menara Alpha: an old student favourite, fully refurbished.
videoTitle: PROPERTY REVIEW #422 | MENARA ALPHA, WANGSA MAJU
excerpt: An older two-tower block a short walk from Wangsa Maju LRT and TAR UMT, where one owner rebuilt a 1,300 sq ft unit. Sean admires the density and the rent, but warns that refurbishing costs a lot.
takeaways: Units of about 1,300 sq ft list for RM320,000 to RM380,000, and a whole unit rents for about RM3,000.
Low density: two towers of about 700 units, with more than 60% of the land used for ground-level parking.
Old pipes, wiring and layouts mean a full refurbishment can cost RM150,000 to RM200,000.

sections.heading: What sets it apart
paragraphs: Menara Alpha is an older building of two blocks with about 700 units in total, ground-level covered parking and simple facilities: a pool, a badminton court, a playground and a coffee shop. Each corridor serves two floors, with short stairs up or down to the units, so one lift lobby serves 36 units.

Sean viewed a corner unit of about 1,300 sq ft with three bedrooms plus a master bedroom. With the management's consent, the owner pushed the window line out over the old balconies, rebuilt the kitchen, bathrooms, windows and wiring, and The Makeover Guys handled the decoration.

sections.heading: Where it is
paragraphs: The block stands behind the shop lots outside Wangsa Maju LRT station, opposite TAR UMT and next to a school, among low-rise government housing. Street food, mamak restaurants, malls, hospitals and colleges are close by, and the new SPE highway has shortened the drive to KL city centre.

sections.heading: Rent and returns
paragraphs: Listings ask about RM320,000 to RM380,000 for a 1,300 sq ft unit, and this refurbished unit is let whole for about RM3,000 a month. Sean estimates the instalment on a RM300,000 purchase at roughly RM1,300 to RM1,400 plus maintenance, but a run-down unit could need about RM80,000 for furnishing and another RM80,000 for utilities, and he puts this owner's spend at RM150,000 to RM200,000.

standout.title: One corridor for two floors
standout.body: Each double-height corridor serves units half a floor above and half a floor below it, and one lift lobby connects three such corridors. Sean calls it remarkably efficient, close to 100% of the floor sold, and notes the open panels ventilate it better than many modern buildings.

pros: The location, which he knows from his own A-level years there: everything was walkable, with the LRT, shuttle buses, food and shops, and today it is a mature address with schools, malls, universities, medical centres and the new SPE highway.
The density: more than 60% of the land given to ground-floor parking and only about 700 units in two towers, which he says you can't find any more.
The investment case: a large tenant pool of students and nearby workers, and rents that make sense against what owners paid.
cons: The immediate setting: the entrance runs through busy shop lots at a traffic-light junction with illegal parking, the school bells next door ring through the day, and the student crowd is noisy late at night.
It is an old building: corridors flood in heavy rain, facilities are minimal, piping and wiring need replacing, and big beams and columns make the rooms awkward.
The cost of refurbishing: spending about RM150,000 on a RM300,000 unit to rent it for RM3,000 makes the return only so-so, and it takes passion, time and coordination as well as money.

closing: A low-density, well-located old block that can be transformed, but only for owners with the passion and capital to rebuild a unit properly.
sourceNote: Based on Sean's full English captions for this January 2026 episode and its video description. The 3 on 3 follows the three things he likes and the three he doesn't, in his order, at the end of the video. An owner let Sean view the refurbished unit; listing prices and rent are as he quoted them, and the instalment and refurbishment costs are his estimates. Sean studied nearby, and The Makeover Guys, where he works, decorated the unit.
